headline: Satellite investments surge. Space debris looms. Robotics power up.
deck: This week sees record satellite funding, debris cleanup efforts, and robotics partnerships.

stories.head: Satellite investments hit $8.1 billion halfway through 2026
stories.body: Satellite investments reached a staggering $8.1 billion in the first half of 2026, setting a new annual record. This surge suggests that investors are increasingly betting on the orbital economy as a lucrative frontier. With companies like True Anomaly and Astranis securing significant funding, the trend shows no signs of slowing.
stories.soWhat: If this keeps up, we might soon see more satellites than stars in the sky, which is both amusing and slightly alarming.

stories.head: Florida startup SOAR targets space debris cleanup
stories.body: Florida-based startup SOAR is partnering with the University of Texas to develop a passive system aimed at trapping small space debris. This initiative highlights the growing recognition that space litter is a serious issue, with potential costs mounting as more satellites and debris clutter the orbits. The details on how effective this system will be remain to be seen.
stories.soWhat: Cleaning up space might soon become the next gold rush, but the real question is whether anyone can make money doing it.

stories.head: Icarus Robotics selects KULR for Space Station battery needs
stories.body: Icarus Robotics has chosen KULR to provide batteries for its robots operating on the International Space Station. This collaboration underscores the importance of reliable power sources in space, especially as robotic roles expand in complex environments. Financial terms weren't disclosed, but the partnership indicates a strategic move in the robotic supply chain.
stories.soWhat: Even robots in space can't afford to run out of juice; this partnership might just keep them from having a meltdown—literally.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
